value.overview: The Royal Tern (Thalasseus maximus) is a large coastal seabird of the Americas and one of the biggest terns, exceeded in size mainly by the Caspian Tern. It is recognized by its long, pointed wings, deeply forked tail, black shaggy crest, white body, and heavy orange bill with a darker tip. Royal Terns usually forage over shallow marine waters and rest in groups on beaches, sandbars, islands, and other open coastal sites.
value.classification: The Royal Tern belongs to the tern family Laridae and the order Charadriiformes. It is one of the large crested terns in the genus Thalasseus.
value.identification: Adults are large, slim-bodied terns with a white head and underparts, pale gray wings and back, a black crown and shaggy rear crest, and a long forked tail. The thick, orange bill is a strong identification feature. In nonbreeding plumage, the black on the forehead may recede, leaving more white on the crown. Juveniles are duller and may show darker markings on the wings and back. Its flight is powerful and buoyant.
value.rangeHabitat: The Royal Tern occurs along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the Americas, from the southern United States and the Gulf of California through the Caribbean and Central America to northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a coastal species recorded along both the Pacific and Caribbean shores, especially near beaches, estuaries, bays, offshore islands, and other shallow marine habitats. It is generally found close to shore, although individuals may occasionally occur farther offshore.
value.migrationStatus: Royal Terns are partly migratory and dispersive. In Costa Rica they occur mainly as nonbreeding visitors and coastal year-round birds, with records in multiple months; they are not generally known to breed there. Birds using Costa Rican waters may move seasonally along the Pacific or Caribbean coasts.
value.breeding: Royal Terns breed colonially on low, open coastal islands, sandbars, beaches, and other predator-free sites. The nest is usually a shallow scrape on bare ground or shell-covered substrate. Typically one egg is laid, although clutch size can vary. Both adults incubate and defend the nesting area, and chicks gather in creches after hatching while adults continue to feed them. Colonies are often mixed with other terns and seabirds.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small marine fish, supplemented by squid, shrimp, and other aquatic prey. Royal Terns commonly feed by flying over the water and plunging headfirst to seize prey beneath the surface. They may also take food near the surface or accept prey brought by another bird. Feeding is concentrated around productive coastal waters, tidal channels, bays, and areas where fish gather.
value.behavior: Royal Terns are social and often rest, roost, and travel in flocks. They give loud, harsh calls around colonies and roosts. Courtship includes head movements, calling, posturing, and presentation of fish. Outside the breeding season, they may associate with other large terns and gulls. They are strong fliers and can cover substantial distances while following coastlines or searching for schools of fish.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely quantified, but the species remains widespread and is not currently assessed as globally threatened.
